articles.title_orig: Fate unknown of many returned to DPR Korea from China: UN independent experts
articles.title_zh: Fate unknown of many returned to DPR Korea from China: UN independent experts
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Three years on from the reported resumption of large-scale forcible returns of nationals of the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) from China, serious concerns persist about their fate, according to a group of Human Rights Council-appointed independent experts.
There is no information on the whereabouts and treatment of those repatriated – or those who remain at risk of return – the experts said in a press release on Wednesday.
“ These events form part of a longstanding pattern of serious human rights violations against individuals forcibly returned to the DPRK . In the absence of independent monitoring in either country, many returnees remain unaccounted for,” they said.
“For as long as their fate and whereabouts remain unknown, returnees are deprived of essential safeguards against enforced disappearance, arbitrary detention, execution, torture, forced labour, sexual and gender-based violence and other serious human rights violations,” the experts added.
Reports indicate that some women who left the DPRK – commonly known as North Korea – became victims of trafficking, forced marriage and sexual exploitation.
Among them is Kim Cheol-ok, who reportedly fled the DPRK during the 1990s famine and was trafficked into China as a child.
Forced into marriage at 14, she was subjected to sexual violence and forced pregnancy.
Despite living in China for about 25 years and establishing family ties, she reportedly faced harassment and restrictions due to her irregular status.
Detained by Chinese authorities in April 2023 without access to legal representation, she was forcibly returned in October 2023. Her fate and whereabouts remain unknown.
The Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found in 2024 that her detention by China and the DPRK was arbitrary.
Since 2023, reports have emerged of serious human rights violations against returnees, particularly those perceived as having sought asylum or who left the country without authorisation , raising concerns under the principle of non-refoulement.
The principle states that no one should be returned to a country where they face a real risk of persecution, torture or inhuman treatment.
“ Irregular migration status does not diminish the obligation to respect the principle of non-refoulement,” the experts said.
“Given longstanding evidence that DPRK nationals who leave the country without authorisation, or seek protection abroad, may face severe punishment upon return,” they said, the reported mass returns “raise questions about whether their protection needs were adequately assessed before repatriation”.
The experts said “ persistent obstacles continue to impede efforts to obtain information ” on the fate and whereabouts of returnees – including those in political prison camps – as well as those who remain at risk of forcible return from China.
They called on China to respect the principle of non-refoulement, refrain from repatriating North Koreans “and ensure access to fair and effective procedures for assessing their international protection needs”.
They also called on Pyongyang to disclose the fate and whereabouts of returnees.
Special Rapporteurs and other independent experts are appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva to monitor and report on specific human rights themes or country situations.
They serve in their individual capacity, are independent of any government or organization, are not UN staff and receive no salary for their work.

articles.title_zh: Meta earnings live: Meta Q3 earnings to test Wall Street's stomach for AI spending
articles.content_orig:
A big rally in SpaceX after earnings is giving hope to Meta and Tesla bulls ahead of their reports due Wednesday afternoon.
Options trading in both stocks leaned bullish after the open Wednesday, with Meta options looking particularly one-sided as traders bought more calls than puts and more put trades likely initiated by sellers than buyers. More than 30,000 calls traded at or above the ask, suggesting they were bought, versus under 17,000 puts, Cboe LiveVol data shows.
Meta options have generally been bullish since the stock's March low, when the put/call ratio of open contracts plunged to 0.5, meaning two calls open for every one put contract, and that hasn't budged much since, Barchart data show. Almost $22 million of trades were done with a bullish intent on Wednesday, compared to $7.5 million looking for downside.
Market-makers are pricing a 6.5% swing for Meta after earnings, a little under the 9% average the past four quarters. The most popular contract to buy on Wednesday was the 800 strike call expiring Friday that costs $1.40 and needs Meta to rally 14% into the weekend, SpotGamma data shows.
In Tesla, the flows also lean bullish, but with less conviction. The put/call ratio of open contracts is 0.75, compared to Meta's 0.5, though more calls did trade Wednesday morning than puts.
Of the 520,000 contracts traded in Tesla, 315,000 were calls, as traders bought 88,000 calls and 65,000 puts, according to Cboe LiveVol data. There was also notable call-selling, with 83,000 call contracts likely sold and seven of the top 10 trades by dollar-amount call sales.
Still, traders spent more money buying calls than they did puts, with call-buying premiums amounting to over $200 million, compared to $84 million in puts, according to SpotGamma's analysis.
Market-makers are pricing a 5.5% swing in Tesla after its report, above the four-quarter median of 3.5%. That said, Tesla's last report caused a 14% selloff in the stock that makes the average move in that period 5.5%.
The most-heavily traded contracts by volume Wednesday were the 385 and 400-strike calls expiring Friday, with buyers favoring the cheaper 400-strike call and sellers leaning into the 385-strikes, SpotGamms data show.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi issued a warning to the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, saying it should choose diplomacy over returning to war.
"Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance if we see strong evidence of a sincere desire by US to build trust & reach a just solution," he wrote on X , sharing a link to an opinion piece in the Financial Times. "But if US chooses war over diplomacy, it'll certainly result in an even greater strategic failure."
Araghchi said earlier in the day that Iran and the U.S. were still involved in indirect negotiations via mediators over the seven-day ceasefire proposal from September. The proposal was outright rejected by President Trump, but Araghchi said the U.S. was trying to add further clauses to the agreement.
The U.S. Treasury announced new sanctions on the Panamanian-Greek law firm Karnakis and Karnakis for involvement in Iran's "shadow fleet" as part of its Operation Economic Outcast .
The U.S. accuses Karnakis and Karnakis of being indirectly involved in Iran's illicit shipping operations for years. A "shadow fleet" refers to oil tankers that hide their true ownership in order to evade sanctions.
"Whether you are conducting illegal oil transfers at sea or sitting in the corner office of a law firm, if you are supporting the Iranian regime, we will find you and sanction you," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. "Iran's facilitators must make a choice: Either you are with us or against us. We know who you are, we know what you're doing, and we will continue to take action."
The Treasury also said it sanctioned Singapore- and UAE-based shipping agents, including a fleet of cargo vessels that has directly taken part in Iran's "shadow fleet" and "helped generate substantial revenue for the Iranian regime."
A limited number of Saudi airlines took off and landed at the country's main airport on Wednesday, two days after authorities notified airlines that they could resume operations with prior permission.
Saudia and FlyNas were operating flights Wednesday, according to flight-tracking data published by FlightAware. Major carriers, including Lufthansa and Air France, have canceled flights through mid-November.
Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport has been hit multiple times this month by Yemen's Houthi rebels and shut down on Oct. 10. A strike two weeks ago killed 13 people and injured hundreds more.
The Houthis have acknowledged attacking the airport, claiming without evidence that Saudi Arabia provided military equipment to government forces through the facility.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said any interference in the Yemen war by Egypt or any other country would make the situation "more difficult."
"Egypt has sufficient experience to avoid entangling itself in such a highly complex conflict," said Iran's top diplomat in an interview with Iraqi state broadcaster Al-Iraqiya aired on Tuesday.
"We believe that any foreign presence or interference will only make resolving this issue more difficult," Araghchi noted.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Wednesday that Cairo's proposed military support for Riyadh was to "defend Saudi territory, and does not include an attack on Yemen," according to a statement from his office.
At a government event titled Egypt Forum 2026, Sisi said the "objective is to defend the kingdom's lands and borders, as well as those of any other Arab state, should it be requested of Egypt," his spokesman said in a statement.
Sisi on Saturday had asked parliament to authorize support for Saudi Arabia in its war with the Houthis, "if requested."
The parliament, which is stacked with supporters of the president, has since held two rare secret sessions, before postponing deliberations until next week.
Iran's newly appointed defense minister, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, said Wednesday his first hours in office were devoted to meeting the requirements of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Aerospace Force and the army's air defense units.
"We are not in a war of rhetoric in response to repeated threats; we are turning threats into greater readiness and more effective defensive power," he wrote in his first post on X since taking office.
Akhlaghi added Iran was concentrating on its objectives through the use of new technologies.
"We may eat dirt, but we will not give up our soil," he concluded.
President Trump blocked a planned Israeli multiday operation that would have resumed strikes against Iran on the weekend of Oct. 10, according to the Financial Times .
The plan was designed to exceed the intensity of the joint U.S.-Israeli military offensive launched in February, three people familiar with the matter told the paper, and would have struck Iranian nuclear sites, regime targets and civilian infrastructure such as power plants.
The president blocked the strike to avoid escalating conflict before the U.S. midterm elections, according to the report.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Wednesday he had directed the Israeli army and intelligence services to topple the Iranian regime.
"The regime in Iran has still not learned the lesson," Netanyahu told a graduation ceremony at an officer training school in the country's southern Negev desert.
"Mojtaba Khamenei, the current tyrant, has decided to follow in his father's footsteps," he said, referring to the country's supreme leader, who replaced his father Ali Khamenei after he was killed in a U.S.-Israeli airstrike on Feb. 28.
"He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again attempting to develop 'death bombs,'" he added, without giving details on what exactly he was referring to.
"There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all," Netanyahu said, "by toppling the regime in Iran. And that is my directive to the [Israel Defense Forces], the Mossad, and the security services."
He did not expand on how he expected the military or intelligence services to carry out the directive.
Saudi Arabia has held talks with a senior Syrian military delegation on arrangements to transfer up to 10,000 Syrian fighters to take part in the war against Yemen's Houthi movement, according to a report by the Lebanese Hezbollah-owned Al-Akhbar newspaper, citing Yemeni intelligence sources.
The report claims Syrian military officials visited Saudi Arabia's southern regions of Najran and Asir to inspect sites prepared to receive the fighters, while discussions in Riyadh covered transport logistics, financing and military assignments.
The Syrian delegation included Brig. Gen. Khaled Khattab, former commander of the Ansar al-Tawhid faction and current commander of the 82nd Division in the new Syrian army; and Brig. Gen.Haitham al-Ali, also known as Abu Muslim, commander of the army's Third Corps and a former leader in Hayat Tahrir al-Sham.
Khattab reportedly spent four days in southern Saudi Arabia, accompanied by Saudi officers, visiting sites in the regions of Asir and Najran being prepared to receive Syrian fighters. Meanwhile, al-Ali held several meetings with Saudi officers at the Defense Ministry in Riyadh to discuss the costs of transferring around 10,000 fighters, financial arrangements, additional benefits and their intended military tasks. The delegation reportedly finalized logistical arrangements for the transfer.
The report also raises the possibility that foreign fighters currently in Syria, including Uyghurs, Uzbeks, Tajiks and other nationalities, could be transferred to Yemen.

Iranian parliamentarians overwhelmingly approved the appointment of Mehrdad Akhlaghi Ketabchi, 68, as the country's new defense chief on Sunday.

articles.title_orig: China skeptics raise alarm over Hochul's plan for upstate chip plant: 'Red flags here with yellow stars'
articles.title_zh: China skeptics raise alarm over Hochul's plan for upstate chip plant: 'Red flags here with yellow stars'
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — New York Gov. Kathy Hochul’s plan to open a computer chip plant outside Utica is raising concerns among federal officials who fear that China could gain greater access to advanced US technology.
Sources close to the Democratic governor told The Post Tuesday that the governor is in “advanced talks” with Solidigm, a subsidiary of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, to open a semiconductor plant in Oneida County.
“There are red flags here with some yellow stars that the feds are really going to worry about,” quipped a federal official, who accused Hochul of being used to undermine US interests in the artificial intelligence arms race.
Hochul previously had an alleged Chinese spy, Linda Sun, as her deputy chief of staff from 2021 to 2023.
Sources expressed concern about the possibility that Chinese workers at the New York facility would give Beijing a “back door” to US technology and noted that the parent company wants to loosen new Trump administration export rules on chipmaking equipment that can be sent to China.
SK Hynix wants to condition the opening of a new US manufacturing facility on the Commerce Department granting export licenses for advanced equipment for use at a Chinese factory in Dalian, Reuters reported this month.
“It’s very clear why SK wants to do this deal. The Chinese are pressuring them,” said Leland Miller, who serves on the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, a 12-person body formed in 2000 to advise Congress on national security concerns involving trade with China.
“[The Chinese] have been pressuring them for a long time in terms of their operations in China, and Beijing would like to see more of a buildout in China,” Miller said.
“The reason for this is that the Chinese absolutely want to catch up with the Koreans and Americans in terms of memory chip buildout.”
Hochul spokeswoman Kristin Devoe brushed off criticism, saying in an email that “projects like this are required to undergo a comprehensive federal national security review.”
“This company [Solidigm] was founded and is headquartered in the United States and is responding to a directive from the Trump Administration to build what would be America’s only domestic fab of its kind,” she added. “Reshoring this vital technology would mean THOUSANDS more American manufacturing jobs and chips made here instead of overseas.”
The Biden administration in December 2024 offered SK Hynix $458 million in grants and $500 in loans under the CHIPS Act to build a different manufacturing plant in Indiana, which remains under development.
Miller, who is also CEO of China Beige Book, which tracks Chinese economic data, said that the New York manufacturing facility would offer “a back door for the Chinese to be observing advanced memory capacity buildout in action.”
“All these facilities are going to have more advanced IP than what they’ve been exposed to thus far. So they will be moving the needle forward for China, no matter what. The question is how much,” Miller said.
“It’s very clear what’s driving this process. It’s an age-old problem where the Chinese put pressure on companies to say, ‘Look, we want this in return for that,’ and so the possibility that this is going to have negative effects based on exposure to IP is very, very high.”
Solidigm said in a statement that the company “regularly evaluates strategic alternatives to enhance its long-term competitiveness.”
“The company is currently exploring options for building a NAND memory fab at potential locations around the world, including the U.S. No decision regarding any specific course of action has been made,” the company said.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Opens Higher; SpaceX Shares Surge on Tesla Deal Talks — Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Opens Higher; SpaceX Shares Surge on Tesla Deal Talks — Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX stock jumped 10% Wednesday after the company reported surging revenue growth in its third quarter, and owner Elon Musk floated a potential SpaceX- Tesla merger.
The space company, which made its debut on the Nasdaq in the biggest initial public offering ever in June, reported third-quarter revenue on Tuesday of $14.6 billion, up 161% from the previous year, and beating LSEG consensus estimates of $12.72 billion.
Meanwhile, its operating income came in at $2.8 billion, with net income of $4.4 billion, after reporting a net loss of $1.05 billion in the same period a year earlier.
On an earnings call, Musk said he's considering a combination with Tesla — which would mark the largest merger in history — and that the boards of both companies have created specific committees to discuss a consolidation.
"I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained from cooperating," Musk said on the call. Tesla is set to report third-quarter earnings after the closing bell on Wednesday.
Shares of other space stocks, including Rocket Lab , Intuitive Machines and AST SpaceMobile climbed on Wednesday.
SpaceX forecasts first-quarter 2027 revenue between $33 billion and $37 billion, beating the average analyst estimate of $22.2 billion, according to LSEG.
"We delivered another strong quarter in Q3. Revenue grew an impressive 161% year-over-year, fueled by continued momentum in Connectivity and a clear inflection in our Super Intelligence business," SpaceX's chief financial officer, Bret Johnsen, said in the earnings release.
Johnsen pinned the strong results on recurring revenue from its satellite internet business, Starlink , and significant expansion of its Super Intelligence [SI] infrastructure.
The company has dived into artificial intelligence this year, which it's now calling SI. The segment is its largest business unit, with revenue soaring ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year.
Commentary on computing during the earnings call supported "continued pricing power and shorter payback periods" for AI cloud providers, Truist Securities analysts said in a Tuesday note.
"Despite market concerns relating to financing for AI cloud providers this past week, we believe SpaceX's third-quarter 2026 represents the first data point during the earnings season to support the bull case for AI cloud providers," they added.
They explained that demand appears "insatiable," with SpaceX noting that it could rent out its capacity several times over. The analysts said Coreweave and Nebius are set to benefit and capture demand as "pricing power will more than offset higher rates."
The shares of neoclouds Nebius and Coreweave traded marginally lower, while Iren and Applied Digital climbed in early trading on Wednesday.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion for Deceiving Users on Privacy
articles.title_zh: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion for Deceiving Users on Privacy
articles.content_orig:
Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
CNBC has reached out to Meta for comment on the penalty order.
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.

articles.title_orig: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.title_zh: Just Eat apologises for AI food mistakes after social media ridicule
articles.content_orig:
Just Eat has apologised after it was ridiculed online over a series of mistakes with AI-generated pictures for some of its restaurants' food items.
The online food delivery platform had been testing out the tech to showcase food which didn't have images yet - but not all turned out as planned.
Instead the AI invented several bizarre concoctions, from bacon and eggs floating in a glass of cola - a confusion between "soda" and "soda bread" - to chips poking out of muffins.
A Just Eat spokesperson said the firm was "in the process of removing" the incorrect images, and would stop making more until the AI was further developed.
"We work with tens of thousands of small restaurants on their food imagery, including funding professional local photographers," the spokesperson told the BBC.
"We've been trialling AI-enhanced images, and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time."
The incident highlights the difficulties companies can still face when using AI to speed up or simplify work processes, especially when it is used to interpret words in a specific context.
Members of the Just Eat UK subreddit have flocked to the site over the past few days to post the latest unintentionally hilarious spins on takeaway food items.
Any picture generated using AI on the delivery app appears with a label indicating so, and the BBC has spotted many of the more unusual takes still up on menus.
A Belfast cafe, meanwhile, had its bacon and egg soda bread dish represented as a glass of fizzy drink with a cooked egg and bacon floating in it.
Spelling mistakes on menu items have sometimes added to the confusion, with the Instagram account @uknewestfoods posting a picture of garlic bread in the shape of a plane - presumably because of a misspelling of the word "plain".
Meanwhile, a "cheese roll" - bread and cheese - instead became slabs of cheese rolled into a sushi roll.
While some on social media said they found the images "hilarious", another was less interested in the AI-generated dishes, saying: "Well, that lot just helped my diet".
Meanwhile, one person on Instagram questioned why customers would ever want to see AI images of a restaurant's food even if they were closer to the real thing.
"I want to see what the dish actually looks like as it helps me decide who to order from or what to order," they said.
"These 'perfect' AI versions just lead to disappointment if that's what you think your meal will look like."

articles.title_zh: Buffett’s Berkshire just trounced chip stocks and flashed a rare dot-com-era signal
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
For three weeks, Wall Street sold the hottest trade in the market and bought one of the oldest. Chip stocks lost 15% while Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway gained 7%.
That swing carried Berkshire's Class B stock ( BRK-B ) to a record close Tuesday, its first since May 2, 2025 — the day before Buffett said he would hand the CEO job to Greg Abel. The stock pushed to an intraday record Wednesday, as did the Class A stock ( BRK-A ).
The wait took 17 months, a stretch in which the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained more than 35%.
From Oct. 6 through Tuesday, the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) fell in 10 of 11 sessions. Berkshire rose on nine of those days, and on chips' two worst days, Oct. 14 and Oct. 16, it posted two of its best gains of the run.
For now, that price action has made Berkshire look like a hedge against the AI chip trade. Since Oct. 1, it has mostly risen on the days chips fell.
Berkshire is on track to rise in 14 of its last 15 sessions. Along the way, it strung together a 10-day winning streak, its first since 2018, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
From Oct. 2 through Tuesday, Berkshire beat SOXX by 22 percentage points. That's the widest gap over any 12-session stretch since early 2010, according to Yahoo Finance calculations that compare Berkshire with the PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) back to 1994. The 12-session window is the one that captures this month's widest gap.
The rarer signal is the combination.
Chips fell at least 14% while Berkshire gained at least 7% over 12 sessions. Before this month, that last happened Oct. 3, 2001. Every earlier case came in 1995-96 or in 2000-01, the latter as the dot-com bubble burst.
History sends a mixed message from here.
In the near term, chips bounced. They were higher a week later in five of the six earlier cases, and they're rebounding Wednesday,too. A year out, chips were lower in five of six instances, and the S&P 500 fell in four.
Four of those six cases came during the same bear market, though. Treat this as a rare signal, not a forecast.
Abel has also changed how Berkshire uses its cash. Berkshire bought back about $4.5 billion of its own stock in the second quarter and ended 14 straight quarters of net stock selling while its cash pile fell from a record $397 billion.
Buffett said Sept. 18 he would also step down as chairman. The stock bottomed two weeks later.
The next test comes with third quarter results, expected to be released Saturday, Nov. 7.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX will attempt to reach weekly Starship launches by early 2027
articles.title_zh: SpaceX will attempt to reach weekly Starship launches by early 2027
articles.content_orig:
In its current iteration, SpaceX is largely a data company seeking to provide enormous amounts of compute for artificial intelligence. During an earnings call on Tuesday afternoon, company officials spent much of their time discussing ambitious plans to roll out up to 10 GW of compute in 2027—on the ground.
Gone are the days of aspirational talk about sending humans to Mars and settling the red planet. Now it is almost all about artificial intelligence and the data needed to support its expansion. However, the company’s long-term ambitions to provide data services from space, initially with the Starlink Internet constellation and eventually through the “Starmind” data center constellation, still rely on an actual rocket.
That would be the Starship vehicle, and during the earnings call, SpaceX founder Elon Musk and the company’s president and chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, provided new performance targets for the vehicle.
It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test, Musk said, to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight.
Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures. Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight.
One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico.
“We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” Shotwell said.
As for what comes after this test flight, Shotwell said SpaceX would attempt to refly a Starship upper stage “early” next year. The company will also seek to complete a long-delayed refueling test of Starship early in 2027. This Starship-to-Starship refueling demonstration is an important milestone for SpaceX and NASA to prove the viability of Starship being refueled in low-Earth orbit for lunar missions.
Refueling on this scale has never been done before, and the company needs to get data on the efficiency of such transfers and the rate of boil-off of liquid oxygen and methane in space. This data will refine projections for how many launches are needed to support a Starship landing on the Moon for NASA as part of the Artemis Program.
For SpaceX, the near-term priority is reaching a high flight cadence for Starship and pushing the boundaries of vehicle reuse to enable it.
Musk, who often offers hyper-optimistic timeframes, said he expects Starship to reach a “weekly” flight cadence during the first half of 2027 and to launch twice weekly during the second half of the year. The key will be how much Starship can be reused.
“The rate at which we launch Starship will increase dramatically as we solve rapid and complete reusability,” Musk said. “At first there will be a little bit of refurbishment that’s needed between each flight, and we’ll iron out the need for any refurbishment such that you can immediately land the rocket and launch it again, just like an airplane.”
That’s the vision, at least. Achieving complete reusability with an orbital rocket has never been done before, so SpaceX’s engineering team will undoubtedly face some significant hurdles. Over time, however, they are likely to get close to the vision of launching, landing, and reflying rockets.
SpaceX will largely focus on its own payloads in 2027 with the Starship rocket. Shotwell said the company would continue launching Starlink V3 satellites, the second generation of “mobile” satellites that deliver direct-to-cell connectivity, as well as Starmind data center prototypes, next year. During the earnings call, neither Musk nor Shotwell addressed, nor were asked by financial analysts, about the controversial throttling of Starlink capabilities for Ukraine in its war with Russia.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Senators Express ‘Grave Concerns,’ Launch Inquiry into Google’s AI Push in Schools
articles.content_orig:
The letter asks Google CEO Sundar Pichai to respond by Nov. 2 on what the company knows about AI's effect on students
Kevin Carter / Getty Images
Sens. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, and Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, sent a letter to Google $GOOGL CEO Sundar Pichai asking what the company knows about how its AI products affect the mental health of kids and their growth as learners, according to The Wall Street Journal .
The senators wrote that they have "grave concern" that Google 's "aggressive push of A.I. products to children in schools is threatening the academic success and overall wellbeing of an entire generation." They set a Nov. 2 deadline for Google to reply.
The letter asks Pichai how much Google understands about the ways its AI tools might harm children, why AI features were made the default setting on school devices, which worries districts, teachers and parents have voiced about students leaning on AI academically and emotionally, and which promotions Google has used to broaden the use of AI in schools.
" Google is forcing their A.I. products into classrooms across America, and children are paying the price," the senators wrote, according to The Wall Street Journal. "We cannot repeat the mistakes of social media platforms where products are pushed onto children putting profit ahead of young peoples' best interest."
The letter cites a September Wall Street Journal investigation. Drawing on more than 60 conversations with educators, school officials, parents, students and clinicians, the investigation found that many students have grown emotionally and academically reliant on Google 's AI tools, according to The Wall Street Journal. The Journal also spoke with current and former Google staff and examined the company's research papers, which showed that Google 's own researchers have cautioned that the technology can carry heightened risks for children and may cause cognitive and emotional harm, according to The Wall Street Journal.
A Google spokesperson pointed The Wall Street Journal to a statement the company issued previously, which read “teachers around the world use our technology every day because it solves real classroom challenges and helps improve learning outcomes.” The statement said Google develops its products by working alongside educators and leaves teachers and administrators in charge of how they are used. Google has said it promotes critical thinking and built safeguards aimed at users younger than 18, among them steps meant to head off emotional dependence, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Slipping test scores have driven a backlash against classroom screen time among people of all political stripes, according to The Wall Street Journal. Parent anger has prompted districts such as New York City and Los Angeles to suspend AI use by students in their classrooms through moratoriums, according to The Wall Street Journal.
Chromebooks make up roughly 59% of the devices in U.S. schools, according to Crypto Briefing . By early October, Google had extended access to its Gemini student hub to every K-12 user on Google Workspace for Education, according to Crypto Briefing.
In a July report, Common Sense Media found that the AI tools built into Google Search, such as AI Overview and AI Mode, present an “unacceptable risk” to kids, according to Crypto Briefing. A Senate HELP subcommittee convened on Oct. 9 to examine how AI is affecting K-12 education, according to Crypto Briefing.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.title_zh: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
articles.content_orig:
Person named ‘K’ from China paid five defendants to injure Huang Yi-hao, New Taipei prosecutors say
Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping .
Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary.
In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record.
Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation.
The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.”
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment.
A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said.
The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.
K refused to pay the full sum of NT$450,000 (US$13,900; £10,370) promised to the suspects because Huang’s injuries were only minor, the statement said.
On Wednesday, Huang reposted a video from December 2025 in which he asked the audience to help him by shouting out the name of the person he was about to describe.
In a fast-paced diatribe, the comedian, dressed in a traditional gown, evoked “swept-back hair” and a “plump figure”, and criticised policies on Hong Kong, Covid and the property market. After finishing with an expletive, the crowd chanted back Xi’s name before breaking into applause.
In May, two people were prosecuted after spreading faeces and paint at a Taipei club hours before a Huang show.
Lev Nachman, a professor of political science at National Taiwan University, said: “It is important to remember that what we are reading about is obviously a more extreme case, but there have been threats and acts of violence against critics of the Communist party here in Taiwan for many years.”
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council said in October that at least 126 individuals had been affected by Chinese transnational repression.
The Guardian has contacted the Chinese foreign ministry for comment.
In a post on Wednesday, Huang said: “If people can be subjected to this kind of treatment simply for criticising the Chinese Communist party when it does not even govern Taiwan, how can we expect to retain our current freedom of speech if the CCP were ever to rule Taiwan?”
In another post on Facebook, Huang said he would not cancel future performances but that he was “no hero”.
“I write it because it’s funny,” he said. “If I stop, it will only be because I’ve got bored of it.”

On SpaceX's earnings call late Tuesday, CEO Elon Musk , who also runs Tesla , took a break from talking about financial results to tell investors that it would be a "good idea" to merge his two companies, and said the boards at both have formed special committees to discuss a possible tie-up.
Musk will be back in public after market close on Wednesday, this time to discuss Tesla earnings.
Here's what Wall Street is expecting, according to estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
Should Tesla fail to top expectations, the company would see a slight decrease in revenue from $28.1 billion a year earlier. Tesla has recorded double-digit growth in each of the two prior quarters, but revenue dropped in three of four quarters in 2025, as Chinese EV makers such as BYD and Xiaomi gained popularity in Asia and Europe with affordable and innovative EVs. Tesla was also hit last year by the end of a federal EV tax credit.
Earlier this month, Tesla reported vehicle deliveries for the third quarter of 486,532, about 2% below the year-ago number. Deliveries are the closest approximation of sales reported by Tesla but are not precisely defined in its shareholder communications.
While Tesla still counts on auto sales for the bulk of its revenue, Musk sees the company's future in robotaxis and humanoid robots. That's putting the focus on capital expenditures, which are expected to top $25 billion this year, based on a prior forecast, up from about $8.5 billion in 2025.
One of Tesla's big investments is in a semiconductor factory that it's building with SpaceX and Intel in Grimes County, Texas. That partnership with SpaceX along with other areas of overlap, including work on Tesla's recently announced Roadster refresh, fueled intensifying speculation that Musk's companies were on the verge of combining in what would be a historic transaction.
"I feel like I'm tap dancing through a minefield," Musk said on the SpaceX earnings call, responding to a question about a potential merger.
"Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes," Musk said. "But at the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this." On the Tesla side, that means needing a 50% vote of all shares, which is "quite a high hurdle," he said.
Musk pointed to the company's potential to cooperate on AI software, chip design, Terafab and robotics. Tesla is already using Grok AI technology, developed by SpaceX, to power AI assistants in customer cars, and to help control the company's Optimus humanoid robots now in development.
Tesla's stock price is down 14% this year, after rallying on Wednesday, underperforming all of its megacap tech peers. SpaceX went public in June, and is up from its $150 IPO price after its post-earnings pop.
Tesla CFO Vaibhav Taneja told investors on the company's last earnings call in July that automotive margins had been challenged this year by rising interest rates and energy costs.
But he also touted growing revenue from Full Self-Driving (Supervised), sometimes referred to as FSD, the partially automated driving system Tesla sells for $99 per month. FSD doesn't make Tesla vehicles safe to use without a human driver, and the company markets the system as Assisted Driving in Europe. Taneja said Tesla reached close to 1.5 million paid FSD customers globally as of the end of June.
Investors submitted questions online ahead of Wednesday's call, and one of the top-voted requests was for updates on FSD and when it could become "unsupervised," making customers' vehicles fully automated and safe to use like a robotaxi.
Shareholders also want to hear an update on Tesla's Cybercab, a bronze two-seater designed for use as a robotaxi, but not yet sold to individuals.
Tesla is testing the Cybercab, and has deployed driverless vehicles in a limited U.S. fleet. But the company still lags far behind Alphabet's Waymo in the U.S., and Baidu's Apollo Go in China.

articles.title_orig: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
articles.title_zh: Burnham defends Jackdaw decision as Badenoch urges PM to overturn ban on new oil and gas licences
articles.content_orig:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea amid intense debate about the project's environmental and economic impact.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
But environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused the prime minister of "dithering" on Jackdaw and said a ban on new oil and gas licences should be repealed - but Andy Burnham said her party had "messed up" the original decision.
Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.
A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.
Adura says Jackdaw will provide about 6% of UK gas production, enough to power 1.4 million homes. After imports are included, that amounts to about 2% of total UK demand.
The gas will be pumped to the existing Shearwater platform for processing – known as a tie-back in industry terms – before being piped to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire.
The UK government said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, Jackdaw would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the gas from Jackdaw would be in homes and businesses this month - although she told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast that it would not lower energy bills this winter.
She said the decision would "help minimise the UK's use of imported higher emission fuels as we continue our transition to renewables and nuclear".
"The decision is compatible with our legally binding climate commitments, and we remain resolute in ending new licences for oil and gas and achieving net zero by 2050," she said.
The UK government also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.
At Prime Minister's Questions, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch thanked Burnham for "finally" approving Jackdaw but accused the government of "dithering" over the decision.
She also urged Labour to repeal its ban on all new oil and gas licences.
"We have the resources, the expertise and the people. What we have lost is the confidence to make tough decisions," she said.
The prime minister said he had made a decision that the previous Tory government had "messed up".
He said they had got decisions wrong because they did not give any regard to climate obligations, and that "these things have to be considered in the round".
Burnham also said he had asked the chancellor and energy secretary to look into whether standing charges could be removed from gas bills.
Scotland's First Minister John Swinney said he hoped the announcement would provide some certainty for the north east of Scotland.
"It is vital that the economic benefits of our energy are felt here in Scotland and used to bring energy bills down, rather than flowing to the Treasury to plug more short-term spending gaps," said the SNP leader.
He also welcomed the creation of an energy wealth fund, which he said should be "prioritised for offshore renewable opportunities and be ringfenced to be focused on the north east of Scotland".
Scottish Conservative leader Russell Findlay said the decision was a victory for Scotland's oil and gas workers, but added: "They should never have had to wait this long for common sense to prevail."
Business leaders in Aberdeen said it was "exactly the sort of pragmatic call the North Sea has been crying out for", and unions also welcomed the decision.
But the co-leader of the Scottish Greens, Ross Greer, described the approval as "climate vandalism".
He said: "It is a devastating betrayal of our children's future and it won't even lower energy bills in the here and now."
Environmental campaigners argue that this summer's heatwaves demonstrate the need to tackle climate change by rejecting both Jackdaw and Rosebank.
Areeba Hamid, the co-executive director of Greenpeace, said approving Jackdaw was "the wrong decision" in terms of lowering energy bills, providing energy security, and addressing climate change.
Oxfam said the government had "drilled straight through the UK's climate commitments" and accused the prime minister of sending "the wrong signal as the impacts of climate change intensify".
The charity says the government must commit to not approving any new oil and gas licences, including the proposals for Rosebank.
Jackdaw sits close to the boundary between the British and Norwegian sectors of the North Sea, in an area where Westminster originally granted licences to explore for oil and gas in 1970 and 1989.
The field was discovered in 2005 but it was expensive and technically difficult to exploit.
Shell did not commit to its development until 2022, shortly after the Conservative government had granted consent for production.
But in January 2025, after a challenge by environmentalists, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled that consent for Jackdaw and Rosebank had been granted unlawfully .
The judge, Lord Ericht, said the developers should have provided a more detailed account of the fields' impact on climate change as part of the permitting process.
The judge allowed the companies to continue with preparatory work short of producing oil and gas while they crafted new environmental impact assessments taking into account the eventual effect of actually burning the fossil fuels, not just the emissions which would be created in extracting them.
When BBC News visited the platform this summer, Adura CEO Neil McCulloch said its approval was vital to avoid domestic supply shortages this winter.
However, the UK government has previously suggested that Jackdaw will have little impact on energy security and none on reducing domestic gas and electricity bills.
In August, in an interim response to a consultation on the future of the country's gas supplies, Energy Minister Michael Shanks said the UK would inevitably become more reliant on imports as domestic production declined .
"With diminishing output from the North Sea over the past decades, any gas produced from the UK Continental Shelf represents a tiny fraction of global demand and so will not lower prices nor materially boost supply," wrote Shanks.
Labour has previously said it is opposed to the issuing of new exploration licences but it will consider new production projects if they are tied back to existing facilities.
McCulloch described the Jackdaw decision as "an important and positive step forward" - but said attention now turned to Rosebank.
He has urged the UK government to approve production from the field, in which Adura owns an 80% stake. The other 20% is held by London-based Ithaca Energy.
Rosebank contains an estimated 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.
But while most of Jackdaw's gas is likely to be consumed in the UK, Rosebank's oil will be taken off by tanker and sold on international markets.

articles.title_zh: France Riots Expose the Rage Aimed at Dior, Hermès and Other Luxury Brands
articles.content_orig:
The second-hand online marketplace Vinted has removed listings of looted French goods and stepped up checks on “suspicious” adverts, as the country’s authorities seek to prevent goods stolen during riots from being sold online.
Vinted says its teams have taken “immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting,” following a weekend of unrest that saw shops ransacked across France, with the cost of property damage and theft estimated to be several hundred million dollars.
“The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it,” the company said in a statement, noting that it had “stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings.”
Accounts found to have breached its rules could face permanent bans, Vinted said, adding that it is working with law enforcement and French authorities to “detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour.”
The response comes as the French government increases scrutiny of online marketplaces following reports that goods stolen during Saturday’s unrest were being offered for sale online.
Serge Papin, France’s small businesses minister, said on ​X that authorities had called a meeting Monday with online marketplace operators and officials ​from the interior and justice ministries.
On Tuesday, he said the government had obtained commitments from platforms to detect and remove ads for looted items, and was also monitoring sales itself, warning that anyone selling stolen goods would be tracked down and prosecuted.
Major retailers including luxury groups such as Louis Vuitton and Rolex and beauty retailer Sephora were caught up in the violence, Reuters reported.
Sephora said several of its stores in France had been ransacked, with employees facing “violence, fear and great tension.”
In a statement posted on LinkedIn, the company’s EMEA president, Catherine Spindler, said it had decided to close all its stores at 5pm Saturday and keep its city-center locations closed the following day, for the safety of staff and customers.
“The strength of a company is not its stores or its windows. It is the women and men who keep it alive,” the post reads.
France’s crisis sounds familiar. Is America next?
Luxury fashion brand Burberry also confirmed that its store on Rue Saint-Honoré in Paris was temporarily closed while it assessed the situation.
The emergence of suspected looted goods on resale platforms presents another challenge for retailers already dealing with damage to their stores and disruption to their businesses.
Vinted prohibits the sale of stolen goods and relies on a range of checks, including reports from retailers and users, to identify suspicious listings.
Founded in Lithuania in 2008, Vinted has grown into one of Europe’s largest second-hand marketplaces. France, the UK and Italy are among its biggest markets, according to Reuters.

articles.title_orig: Nearly $1 million worth of rare Pokemon and sports cards stolen from FedEx truck in Orange County heist, police say
articles.title_zh: Nearly $1 million worth of rare Pokemon and sports cards stolen from FedEx truck in Orange County heist, police say
articles.content_orig:
SANTA ANA, Calif. (KABC) -- Nearly $1 million in rare trading cards, including highly valued Pokémon cards, were stolen from a FedEx truck parked near an Orange County business that authenticates and grades the collectible items, according to police.
The theft is the latest in a string of heists involving Pokémon cards, which have exponentially increased in value in recent years.
The Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement on Tuesday that the heist occurred on Oct. 13 outside the Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) office in Santa Ana.
The hundreds of stolen cards are estimated to be worth a total of $963,000, according to police.
"However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined," according to the Santa Ana police statement.
The cards belong to collectors from across the country who submitted them to the PSA to be authenticated and graded.
Two full pallets of collectible cards were stolen, and some cards on a third pallet were also swiped when thieves broke into a FedEx truck, according to police.
"The pallets contained various trading cards, including, but not limited to, sports cards and Pokémon cards," according to the police statement.
Thieves carve hole through drywall to steal high-value Pokémon cards from Anaheim shop
As of Wednesday, no arrests have been announced in the memorabilia rip-off. Police said the investigation is ongoing.
"The value is definitely there," said Gregory Lawrence of Shiny Vault Pokémon Cards. "It's another asset class now. It's not just stocks, bonds, and putting money in the bank. You can put money into cards. Whether it's Pokémon or sports, there is a huge following from across the world."
The theft was first reported by The Athletic, which cited police sources saying the the FedEx truck was broken into during the 60 to 90 minutes the driver was away from the parked vehicle.
"We are aware of a theft involving a third-party shipping vehicle carrying PSA-graded items. We are working closely with law enforcement and the carrier as the investigation continues," Collectors, the parent company of PSA, said in a statement to ABC News.
The company said it deactivated the certificates for the missing cards and has notified its "marketplace partners to be on the lookout for rare and serialized items."
"Our customer service team has contacted affected customers directly and is arranging compensation based on fair market value," the company said. "We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset."
FedEx released a statement to ABC7, saying, "The security of our customers' shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation. Further questions should be referred to local investigators."
One victimized collector, known by his online handle, Sky-B Cards, issued a YouTube video statement , saying the 104 cards he submitted to PSA for grading were among the stolen items. He said he paid more than $8,000 to have the cards graded by PSA and that his cards were insured for more than $150,000.
"These were 104 cards that I've accumulated over two years," Sky-B Cards said in the YouTube video. "There are many irreplaceable cards in here that I will never see again, and honestly that's what hurts the most, outside of being absolutely financially destroyed here."
The heist is the latest in a string of thefts in Southern California and elsewhere in the country of highly valued Pokémon cards, highlighting what appears to be an ever-growing demand for merchandise from the popular childhood card game.
In February, thieves broke into a collectibles shop in Anaheim, by cutting a hole through the wall from a neighboring shop they also broke into, stealing tens of thousands of dollars worth of Pokémon cards.
Captured on video surveillance cameras, the three thieves were seen grabbing hundreds of trading cards and bolting from the shop in less than 10 minutes.
In April, thieves staged a smash-and-grab heist at Elite Sports Cards in Chicago, stealing $100,000 in Pokémon cards, the store owner told ABC Chicago station WLS.
In an interview in April, Jared Mast, president of Mast Wealth Management Group, which deals in alternative investments including collectibles like Pokémon cards, told ABC News the value of Pokémon cards has risen sharply in the past year.
"I would say, collectively, over the last 12 months, things have gone up anywhere from 200 to 300%," Mast said.
Mast explained that Pokémon card value has risen in three different waves over the last decade. First, in 2016, with the arrival of Pokémon Go, the popular mobile game based on the playing cards, and then again in 2019 and 2020, as a generation of celebrities like Logan Paul invested in the collectibles.
ABC News contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Websites taken down across Europe as critical cyber-security update issued
articles.title_zh: Websites taken down across Europe as critical cyber-security update issued
articles.content_orig:
International governments and agencies have urged websites to address two critical cyber-security flaws in a programming language which powers much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities were found within the PHP programming language, with a fix issued on Wednesday afternoon.
Multiple cyber-security agencies have urged organisations unable to apply fixes in time to consider taking their sites down, leaving bodies such as the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC to take pages offline.
The flaws were discovered by AI, with cyber-security firm Wiz saying they were the "most severe vulnerabilities ever discovered" by the tech, which is reshaping the cyber landscape.
Finland has temporarily shut down the government's public web services, while the Netherlands' cyber-security agency said it was taking its own website offline due to the vulnerabilities.
The US National Security Agency issued similar advice on X for organisations to take their systems offline if they were unable to update with the fix.
"These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database," it wrote.
Meanwhile, the White House said federal agencies were working with leading AI labs to speed up a fix to the issue.
And in a post on X , Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
The Wikimedia Foundation, which runs the online encyclopedia Wikipedia, said it was addressing the security vulnerabilities.
"We have taken down a number of other systems as a precautionary measure until they can be safely patched," it said.
That led some people to be unable to access parts of Wikipedia on Wednesday.
Edinburgh council's website has also become inaccessible, as well as the online homes for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
Other websites, including the art platform DeviantArt, have said they are " temporarily down for maintenance " without specifying the reason.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by cyber-security researchers at the firms Calif and Wiz. They used state-of-the art AI, made by OpenAI, to find the flaws.
OpenAI said in a blog post it was "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
According to the firms, they had gone undetected for more than a decade.
"Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours," Wiz said in a blog post.
It has estimated "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to verify that figure.
The Netherlands' National Institute for Public Health and the Environment, an agency of the Dutch government, has taken down its website.
Similarly the website of the Tweede Kamer, the lower house of the nation's parliament, has become inaccessible.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia have urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a note .
Japan's national cyber-security office and EU cyber-security officials have issued a similar warning .
"PHP is everywhere. It ​quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful ⁠lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cyber-security company Huntress said.
Cyber-security expert Don Smith, from the Sophos Counter Threat Unit, told the BBC this would "likely be a priority target" for hackers.
The immediate challenge was not simply installing a patch to fix the issue, but finding and managing every instance where PHP was running, he said.
"The use of PHP is pervasive, it can sit beneath public websites, content management systems, hosting platforms and third-party products, sometimes without even being obvious to the organisation using it," he said.
He said it was crucial that organisations looked out for signs that an attacker "might have already have gained a foothold".
The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said the risk scores given to the vulnerabilities "indicate the potential for unauthenticated remote code execution".
Such a cyber-attack could potentially allow hackers to install malware and take down websites.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, said he was "seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up".
The NCSC said once organisations have installed the update, they should "continuously monitor for security updates from third-party software vendors, including for appliances and services that may bundle PHP".
It is not yet clear which versions of the programming language are affected, but CERT-EU said it could affect all versions of it dating back to PHP 5 onwards - which launched in 2004.
The PHP Foundation has issued the update only for the latest versions however - with people using PHP 8.1 or older being urged to upgrade.
PHP was created for web development. It is used on servers to implement what you see when you visit websites.
Not all websites use it, but it nonetheless powers a large portion of the internet.

articles.title_orig: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.title_zh: AMD Announces FSR 4.1 for Xbox Series X/S, Z2 Extreme and Z2A Handhelds, RX 6000 GPUs and More
articles.content_orig:
Earlier this month AMD senior vice president Jack Huynh told media in South Korea that FSR 4 was coming to more devices, including handhelds - and now that promise has been fulfilled.
Huynh today announced that FSR 4.1 was coming to five new platforms: Radeon RX 6000-series graphics cards; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo mini PCs and mobile workstations; Gorgon Halo and Strix Halo Ryzen 9 laptops; Z2 Extreme and Z2A handhelds like ROG Xbox Ally devices; and Xbox Series X and Series S.
It's a welcome surprise to see AMD's latest generation upscaler on a huge range of extra devices - even though community modders have been working hard to port the technique to an even longer list of supported platforms.
FSR 4, previously known as Project Redstone, is AMD's first machine learning upscaler and offers a significant visual advantage over its earlier efforts at similar frame-rates - hence the interest in making it available on a wider range of PCs, handhelds and other devices. As well as upscaling and anti-aliasing, the tech also includes frame generation and ray reconstruction, giving it better feature parity with Nvidia's similar DLSS tech.
Huynh's announcement also states that FSR is coming to Vulkan, a graphics API that is the default choice for games that don't use (or want to offer an alternative to) DirectX 12. FSR 3 and earlier supported Vulkan, so it's good to see this limitation redressed - though it's not clear how quickly developers will be able to add FSR 4.1 support to their Vulkan games.
More APUs will get FSR 4.1 support in the future, Huynh claimed, and the announcement video also mentions that AMD's next-gen FSR Diamond will be supported on Xbox's Project Helix " family of devices ".
If you want to use FSR 4.1 on your PC (officially) for the first time, you'll need to install Adrenalin Edition version 26.10.1 . The graphics drivers also add support for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Final Fantasy Resonance.

articles.title_zh: Inside Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4: The New Game-Changing Tech Powering Every Mode
articles.content_orig:
Infinity Ward recently opened its Krakow research and development centre to us to showcase the technical advancements powering Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Infinity Ward Poland studio head Michal Drobot was on hand to present debug footage that explained how current-gen hardware on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and PC enables unprecedented visual and systemic upgrades. While a Nintendo Switch 2 version is also launching in parallel via Digital Legends, the core engine focus remains firmly on pushing broader performance and graphical boundaries - including ray-marched smoke and fog, revamped rasterisation techniques informed by path tracing, and a comprehensively reworked animation and movement system.
Let's start with one of the standout additions, a brand new volumetric ray-marched smoke and fog system built exclusively for MW4. Working in tandem with traditional transparencies, this voxel-based solution allows players to interact directly with smoke plumes using gunfire or vehicles. Bullets carve precise temporary holes through the volume - as in Counter-Strike 2 - while sprinting characters displace wisps naturally, all operating within a fixed GPU performance ceiling.
This unified voxel framework extends seamlessly across atmospheric elements, height fog, and overhead clouds, ensuring consistent competitive balance across all online multiplayer and DMZ modes. Server and local client synchronisation guarantees that visual interactions such as lighting, shadows, and smoke dispersion appear identically for every participant. Furthermore, volumetric fog self shadows and interacts dynamically with animated light sources within the environment.
Weather systems also benefit heavily from the new voxel architecture, supporting dynamic transitions between sunshine, rainfall and snow across expansive open maps - a huge change for open-ended modes like DMZ. Snow layers accumulate dynamically on top of existing level geometry, allowing players to gradually reveal the original terrain beneath. Additionally, expanded character and object voxels now track more environmental states than previous games - a great range of variables that coats soldiers in mud, dust, blood or water streaks depending on their movement.
Next there's the new material workflow used in Modern Warfare 4. While full path tracing is reserved for internal visual reference only due to its heavy performance cost - and RT global illumination and RT reflections are PC-exclusive features - MW4 developers chose to heavily optimise rasterisation pipelines, achieving visual results remarkably close to path tracing at a fraction of the computational expense. This strategy ensures the game easily maintains a high frame-rate across a much wider spectrum of hardware, a key consideration given how much of Call of Duty's audience plays on console with 60fps in mind.
A core component of this improved rasterised approach is the neural light grid, which leverages machine learning compression to handle dynamic ambient occlusion and global illumination, a rethought approach that seeks to avoid the typical artefacts caused by screen-space reflections (SSR) and screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO). By storing lighting data more efficiently, light probes can be distributed sparsely across levels without sacrificing visual fidelity. Incidentally, it's an innovation that also helps to reduce the game's installation sizes alongside improved texture streaming techniques.
In part, material rendering receives a major upgrade through custom capture hardware known as the ATVI CT Reflectometer 2.0. By capturing physical surface properties across multiple light gradients, artists are able to access accurate bidirectional reflectance distribution function values for skin, clothing and metallic surfaces. This new material workflow integrates well with the enhanced rasterised ambient occlusion and global illumination passes.
Under the hood, significant optimisations target the entire rendering pipeline through advanced variable rate shading. Variable rate shading dynamically compresses visual data in less critical areas while preserving full native resolution where it matters most, drastically reducing overall graphical overhead - and this time, it's now applied throughout the entire render pipeline, not just for the final rendered pixels. Additional efficiency is gained through multi-resolution transparencies, with effects like smoke scaling in resolution based on distance.
Supporting these techniques, a hybrid rendering setup is also in place: combining traditional forward rendering (F+) with a visibility buffer (V+) for dense geometry. Where it's efficient to do so, parts of the scene will flip from one to the other, with F+ tending to handle triangles nearer the player.
Finally, foundational gameplay mechanics have been completely overhauled alongside these more visual-focused upgrades. Character movement directly influences weapon sway and contextual interactions with walls, while a new physical bullet trajectory simulation replaces older random bloom mechanics.
Together with these technical engineering achievements, Modern Warfare 4 stands as one of the more significant series milestones. It refines the experience for long term fans of the franchise - and impressions from the early access period suggest the campaign at least is one of the series' best in recent memory. We'll have more to say on Modern Warfare 4 to come, including the Switch 2 edition, but for now the outlook on the game's tech is promising to say the least.

articles.title_orig: Smash Bros and Kirby creator Masahiro Sakurai says AI usage will lead to unoriginal and "unprofitable" games
articles.title_zh: Smash Bros and Kirby creator Masahiro Sakurai says AI usage will lead to unoriginal and "unprofitable" games
articles.content_orig:
The use of AI in game development has become a controversial topic across the industry. Some studios are experimenting with the technology to speed up parts of the development process , while others have raised concerns about what greater reliance on AI could mean for creativity and originality. Super Smash Bros. and Kirby creator Masahiro Sakurai has now shared his thoughts, and he believes AI could contribute to an even bigger flood of games that players simply don’t want.
During an interview with Denfaminico Gamer , Sakurai discussed how difficult it has become for developers to create something genuinely original. He pointed out that many modern games are described by comparing them to something that already exists, making it easier for audiences to immediately understand what they are getting.
Sakurai believes creating something original requires taking a different approach. Instead of simply making something similar to what players already know they enjoy, developers have to come up with ideas people may not even realize they want yet. The difficult part is not only finding those ideas, but also convincing a development team or publisher that they can work. AI, however, could make that problem even more noticeable as the number of games being released continues to increase.
Prices correct as of October 9th, 2026.
For example, if Super Smash Bros. had followed the rules of a typical fighting game – 1-on-1 with guarding, attacking, and special moves, and a health system where the match ends with a KO – then I don’t think the first Super Smash Bros. would have even been released.
Even if it had been released, it would likely have been treated as a novelty item, and the history of Super Smash Bros. would have ended there.
Sakurai highlighted Steam as an example of how quickly the market has expanded. When the Game Designers Award was established in 2010, around 275 games were being released on Steam each year. That figure has now climbed to more than 19,000 annually, and Sakurai expects the number to grow further as AI makes it easier to produce games.
“AI will increase the number” of games, he says, but he also remarks that “I think most of them will become unprofitable titles”. The Kirby creator adds, “When it comes to things created with AI… or things mass-produced with poor quality, I think most of them will simply be reproductions of systems seen in various other games.” Hence, they lack the all-important originality.
Likewise, Steam’s latest Next Fest event (the October 2026 edition) is happening right now. The showcase is designed to feature upcoming games by allowing Steam users to access playable demos, but it’s plagued with even more generative AI than last time , with 36% of games coming with an AI disclaimer. In Japan, over 85% of game devs reportedly use AI in some way.
He believes many AI-made games could end up copying ideas and systems that have already proven successful rather than introducing something genuinely new. Sakurai used simple puzzle games as an example, pointing out how one successful concept can quickly lead to numerous similar games. AI could make producing those kinds of imitations even easier.
The game designer also used Fumito Ueda, known for games such as ICO and Shadow of the Colossus, to explain the difference between copying an existing style and creating something new. In Sakurai’s view, AI could potentially study Ueda’s previous games and produce something that resembles them. What it couldn’t do, however, is predict and create whatever entirely new idea Ueda himself might come up with next.

articles.content_orig:
